mappings.note: Defines electrical conductivity and ranks metals by it - a physical property, so LO-1; LO-2's ordering is reactivity ordering only. DEFECT: the stem says 'arrange the following metals' but no list of metals is stored, so that part cannot be answered.
Thermal conductivity as the reason for a choice of cookware metal - LO-1 physical property. No reactivity or corrosion reasoning is required.

Asks for the mechanism of heat conduction through free electrons. LO-1 is the only outcome that owns conductivity, though note the outcome asks students to classify by the property, not to explain it at particle level - recorded as an outcome-scope shortfall.
Asks which physical and chemical properties are used to sort elements into metals and non-metals - this is LO-1 restated almost word for word.

Electropositivity as a defining chemical characteristic of metals, so LO-1. The supporting explanation runs through electron loss and ion formation, which only the competency covers, but the question's demand is the class property.

A self-limiting oxide film stopping further attack is passivation, i.e. corrosion resistance (LO-7). LO-1 was rejected because the item is about why the reaction stops, not about metals reacting with oxygen as a classifier.
States the general metal + dilute acid reaction with examples. A class property with no ranking, so LO-1.

Why metals generally do not combine with hydrogen, argued from metals losing electrons. The subject is a class property of metals (LO-1); the electron-transfer machinery behind it is competency-level.

The metals are named in the stem and the demand is to explain their own behaviour with air and water - LO-1 under the split rule. The sibling items that ask students to NAME the metals that react violently are LO-2, because there the selection is the work.

Explains why a non-metal is placed in the activity series - a question about how the series is constructed, so LO-2. LO-1 is not cited because hydrogen's classification is given in the stem, not asked for.
Contrasts two named metals' occurrence and demands the reactivity reason - a direct ranking of aluminium against gold (LO-2), with no ore processing asked about.
Dulling of aluminium in air by an oxide layer is surface corrosion (LO-7). Grouped with the silver, copper and zinc tarnishing items rather than with metal + oxygen classification.
The decisive clue is that the oxide's solution turns red litmus blue, i.e. a basic metal oxide - LO-1's chemical-property classification. The cement and bone hints are context.

The hydrogen from metal + dilute acid is LO-1, but the collection method, solubility and density questions are laboratory technique, which only C 8.2 reaches; C 8.2-LO-2 is NOT used because no two metals are compared. DEFECT: the stem refers to a figure that is not stored with the item.

The demand is amphoterism - writing the oxide's reactions with both an acid and an alkali - which is LO-1's chemical-property clause. The thermite mention is only an identifying clue for aluminium, so LO-6 is not cited.
Observation and equation for one named metal with dilute acid. Single-substance chemical property (LO-1), not a comparison.
Two candidate displacement equations, only one feasible, and the reason must be the iron/copper ranking - LO-2's predictive clause in its purest form.
Nitric acid's oxidising behaviour as the reason hydrogen is not released. The variable is the acid, not the metals' order, so LO-1. Near-duplicate of an earlier very-short item with the same demand.

Identifies the metal from the formula and molecular mass of its hydroxide plus the flammable gas - a single metal's reaction with cold water (LO-1). No second metal has to be ranked; the arithmetic settles it.
Why aluminium articles resist corrosion, answered by the protective oxide coating - LO-7's corrosion clause, with the oxide layer acting as the prevention mechanism.

WEAK FIT. Solder's constituents plus the low-melting-point property that suits it to welding. Alloy composition and alloy properties have no outcome; LO-7 is cited because alloying is named only there.

Part (i) selects one metal from three by their relative behaviour with cold and hot water (LO-2); part (ii) then wants the equation and product (LO-1). DEFECT: the stored key answers 'iron', but iron reacts with steam and not hot water - the metal that reacts with hot water but not cold is magnesium, and the key's own equation is a steam equation.
Conduction by ionic compounds once melted, explained by freed ions. A compound-property item; no outcome under C 1.1 covers ionic compounds, so the competency is the closest legal code.
Extraction route for metals low in the series, worked through cinnabar to mercury. LO-6 names the reactivity bands itself, so it carries this item alone.

Students must NAME the two metals that catch fire in water, i.e. pick the top of the series, so LO-2. The sibling item that names sodium and potassium in its stem and asks only for the explanation is LO-1.
